Scroll horizontally to inspect cycle-by-cycle execution
Zero hazards detected. Ideal pipeline flow achieved.
Independent instruction %1$s moved ahead to eliminate pipeline stall.

Instruction pipelining divides instruction execution into discrete sub-steps (stages) executed concurrently. In an ideal pipeline with k stages and N instructions, execution approaches 1 instruction completed per clock cycle, giving a theoretical speedup S = (N × k) / (k + N - 1).

4-Stage Model (Chapter 2):
• F (Fetch): Instruction is read from memory.
• D (Decode): Instruction decoding & register reading.
• E (Execute): ALU computation & address calculation.
• WB (Write Back): Result written into register file.

5-Stage Model (TD4 Exercise 6):
• IF: Instruction Fetch
• ID: Instruction Decode & Register Read
• EX: Execution / ALU
• MEM: Memory Access (Load/Store)
• WB: Write Back to Register File

Instruction J reads an operand before instruction I writes it. In an in-order pipeline, RAW is the primary cause of hardware stalls (bulles) because the operand is required in Decode/Execute before Write Back.

Instruction J writes to a register read by earlier instruction I. In standard in-order pipelines, WAR causes ZERO stalls because I always reads in Decode before J commits at WB. However, WAR strictly constrains instruction reordering (compilers must never swap J before I).

Both instructions write to the same destination register. In-order execution naturally preserves the write sequence at WB (0 stalls). However, it prevents compilers from inverting instruction order during reordering.

Caused by branch instructions (JMP, JZ, CALL). The CPU cannot determine the next instruction address until branch resolution, causing pipeline flushes and penalties (2 cycles in 4-stage, 3 cycles in 5-stage per TD4 Ex6).
Occurs when hardware resources are shared and cannot service multiple stages simultaneously (e.g., single memory port for both instruction fetch and data access).
Hardware interlock holds dependent stages idle while earlier stages proceed. Electrically equivalent to executing NOP (No Operation) instructions (Chapter 2 Slide 27).

Hardware multiplexers forward ALU results directly from EX or MEM outputs to the inputs of dependent stages. Notice: Load-Use dependencies still require exactly 1 stall cycle because memory data is only available at MEM stage (TD4 Ex6).
The compiler statically reschedules independent instructions into stall delay slots without altering RAW, WAR, or WAW dependencies, eliminating bubbles at zero hardware cost (Chapter 2 Slide 29).
Predicts branch direction statically (at compile time) or dynamically (via branch history tables) to avoid flushing the instruction stream (Chapter 2 Slide 33).

Engineered specifically to simulate and analyze instruction-level pipelining, x86 register aliasing, cycle chronograms, and hazard resolution techniques aligned with academic examinations and TD series.
